description: Four months of hourly water levels at San Francisco (NOAA CO-OPS station 9414290, the Golden Gate gauge). Signals idea: the Nyquist–Shannon sampling theorem and aliasing. A signal sampled fs times a day can only show frequencies up to fs/2; anything faster is not lost but folded down to |f − k·fs|. The steps read the gauge every 1, 6, 11, 24 and 25 hours (Polars), take the amplitude spectrum of each with a discrete Fourier transform in SQL, and compare its peaks with where alias theory puts the tidal constituents (M2, S2, N2, K1, O1). The aha: read once a day, the 12.42-hour lunar tide becomes a smooth wave of about 14.8 days that is not in the water, and it is as large as the real tide; averaging each day first (a low-pass filter) makes it vanish. This is why every analogue-to-digital converter has an anti-aliasing filter, and why slow, unfiltered monitoring can invent trends. Caveats: the daily-sampled wave's period (14.77 days) is by coincidence close to the real spring–neap cycle (the M2–S2 beat), so don't mistake one for the other; verified heights, in metres above MLLW, times in UTC; the spectrum is a plain DFT on a 0.004 cpd grid without a window, so lines leak a little into their neighbours.
name: Aliasing: a fake two-week tide
